did_you_know.text: Did you know? The chapter opens by addressing the “islands” and “distant nations,” presenting its message as concerning not only Israel but also peoples far away.

Did you know? The servant’s mission is described using two images of weapons: his mouth is like a sharp sword, and he is like a polished arrow. These images emphasize the power and precision of his words.
Did you know? In this verse, the servant is explicitly identified with Israel: “You are my servant, Israel,” and his purpose is to be a source of the LORD’s glory.
Did you know? The servant’s mission does not end with restoring Israel; he is also appointed to be “a light for the nations,” so that the LORD’s salvation may reach the ends of the earth.

Did you know? The LORD describes the recipient as one given as a covenant to the people, whose role is to restore the land and reassign desolate inheritances; thus, redemption also includes the restoration of the land.
Did you know? The returning people are described as being led like a flock: they will not hunger or thirst, and the LORD will guide them to springs of water.

Did you know? The returning people come from various places: from far away, from the north, from the west, and from the land of Sinim. This description emphasizes the gathering of the exiles from every direction.
Did you know? To illustrate the power of the LORD’s memory, Zion is described as engraved on the palms of his hands, with her walls always before his eyes.
Did you know? When the children return, the nations are portrayed as helping Zion: they carry her sons in their arms and her daughters on their shoulders.
Did you know? Even when the captives are held by a mighty warrior or a tyrant, the LORD promises to take them back, contend with Zion’s opponents, and save her children.
